Think how a haploid set compares to a diploid cell - how many copies of each chromosome type are present and what symbol ($n$) is used.
walkthrough:
What Ploidy Really Means**
Think of chromosomes as coming in types. A diploid cell has two sets, so every type is present twice as a homologous pair. A haploid cell has only one set.

Building the Definition**
That is why haploid can be described in two linked ways: one single set, $n$ chromosomes, and no homologous pairs. Each chromosome is different in size, shape and genes carried. Any two of those points earns both marks.
Final answer: Haploid means having a single set of chromosomes ($n$, half the diploid number) with no homologous pairs, so only one of each chromosome type.

Look for where ploidy must change - D is formed by fusion of egg and sperm, so it is diploid and must reduce to make haploid spores.
walkthrough:
Spotting Sexual Reproduction**
Structure C grows into a plant identical to the parent, so that is asexual. Structure B makes sperm that fuses with an egg to form D, giving genetically different offspring, so B and D belong to sexual reproduction.

Where Mitosis Keeps Things Identical**
Mitosis makes genetically identical cells with no change in chromosome number. A and B are parts of the haploid thallus grown by mitosis, C is a mitotic outgrowth that stays haploid and identical, and D also grows by mitosis. Any two of A, B, C, D is accepted.

Where Meiosis Must Happen**
D is the product of fertilisation, so it is diploid while the thallus and spores are haploid. To return to haploid, D must undergo meiosis to produce spores. So D is the site of meiosis.
Final answer: associated with sexual reproduction: B and D; produced by mitosis: any two from A, B, C, D, e.g. A and C; the site of meiosis: D.

walkthrough:
The Doubling Problem**
Horses are diploid ($2n$). If both sperm and egg were diploid, fusion would give $4n$, then $8n$ in the next generation. Chromosome number would double every generation.

Halve Then Restore**
Meiosis includes a reduction division that halves the number from diploid to haploid, producing $n$ gametes. At fertilisation, $n + n$ restores $2n$ in the zygote, so the diploid number is maintained from parents to offspring from generation to generation.

Why Variation and Stability Matter**
That same meiosis creates new combinations of chromosomes and chromatids, giving genetic variation in gametes and therefore genetically different offspring. Without reduction, extra sets would cause developmental problems, infertility or death, so reduction is essential for stable sexual reproduction.

Final answer: Reduction division halves chromosome number to form haploid ($n$) gametes so that fertilisation restores the diploid ($2n$) number in the zygote from generation to generation; this also generates genetic variation in gametes and offspring and prevents harmful extra chromosome sets.
